hints.title: Relative Ordering Boundary Obstacle
hints.text: Rearranging nodes without dedicated sublists risks losing track of boundaries or cyclic links. How can two separate chains simplify separating values less than x from the rest?

hints.title: Dual-Chain Partition Invariant
hints.text: Collect nodes into two independent chains: one for elements strictly less than x, and another for elements greater or equal to x, then splice them.

hints.title: Two-Head Splicing Procedure
hints.text: Create two dummy heads, small and large. Iterate curr through the list, appending nodes with value less than x to small and others to large. Terminate large.next with null and connect small tail to large head. Return small dummy next.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
class Solution:
    def partition(self, head: Optional[ListNode], x: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        small_dummy = ListNode(0)
        large_dummy = ListNode(0)
        small = small_dummy
        large = large_dummy
        curr = head
        while curr:
            if curr.val < x:
                small.next = curr
                small = small.next
            else:
                large.next = curr
                large = large.next
            curr = curr.next
        large.next = None
        small.next = large_dummy.next
        return small_dummy.next
```

variables: N: number of nodes in list (0 <= N <= 200)
complexity.notes: Single pass distributing nodes into small and large chains in O(1) space.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Shuffling nodes within a single pointer chain makes maintaining original relative ordering difficult and error-prone.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Using two dummy heads constructs stable partitions in O(1) auxiliary space without list reallocation.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Ensuring large.next is explicitly terminated with null to prevent circular link references.
